      <title>ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/04/anc-south-africa-local-elections-water-outages-power-cuts</link>
      <description><p>Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts</p><p>The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.</p><p>The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:06:05 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category>Americas</category><title>Democrats warn Trump camp to ‘lawyer up’ as anger over corruption drives midterms wipeout</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20261104-democrats-warn-trump-camp-lawyer-up-anger-over-corruption-drives-midterms-wipeout-gop</link><description>
Corruption in government was high on the minds of US voters as they dealt US President Donald Trump’s party a chastening defeat in midterm elections, toppling Republican strongholds like dominoes and flipping both chambers of Congress. Triumphant Democrats have warned the Trump administration to “lawyer up”; how they go about tackling alleged graft and abuse of power could shape both their own fortunes and the country’s politics.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/4e0e449a-d844-11f1-b10d-1beafce15fea/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-11-02T203404Z-53214534-RC2VFOA5BYP8-RTRMADP-3-USA-TRUMP-LINCOLNMEMORIAL.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/4e0e449a-d844-11f1-b10d-1beafce15fea/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-11-02T203404Z-53214534-RC2VFOA5BYP8-RTRMADP-3-USA-TRUMP-LINCOLNMEMORIAL.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">a2e479f2-d86d-11f1-98c4-893f0c599b14</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:01:05 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/4e0e449a-d844-11f1-b10d-1beafce15fea/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-11-02T203404Z-53214534-RC2VFOA5BYP8-RTRMADP-3-USA-TRUMP-LINCOLNMEMORIAL.jpg">© Umit Bektas, Reuters</source><dc:creator>Benjamin DODMAN</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title><![CDATA['Once-in-a-generation event: Historic election a shocking repudiation of Trump & the MAGA movement']]></title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/once-in-a-generation-event-historic-election-a-shocking-repudiation-of-trump-the-maga-movement</link><description>
Erin Ogunkeye is pleased to welcome Adam Jentleson, President of the Searchlight Institute and author of Supermajority: How Democrats Can Build Lasting Power, For Jentleson, the Democrats' sweeping midterm victory represents far more than the familiar backlash against an incumbent president. "This is a once-in-a-generation event." But electoral breadth presents a governing dilemma. Can a coalition stretching from progressive reformers to culturally conservative Democrats translate its diversity into legislative action? "Pluralism is not just a political strategy. It is actually a moral good in a democracy," he insists. But electoral breadth presents a governing dilemma. Can a coalition stretching from progressive reformers to culturally conservative Democrats translate its diversity into legislative action? And can a party united by opposition to Trump sustain that unity when confronted with difficult choices over healthcare, immigration, economic inequality and climate change?
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/5514019c-d873-11f1-8b6b-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261104-163331-164341-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/5514019c-d873-11f1-8b6b-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261104-163331-164341-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">5a899e02-d873-11f1-9474-5f1065d6543a</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:49:34 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>European leaders welcome Democrats' US midterms election win</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/european-leaders-welcome-democrats-us-midterms-election-win</link><description>
European leaders voiced hopes for a reset with the United States on Wednesday, November 4, after voters delivered a huge midterm election defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican party. FRANCE 24's Dave Keating has more.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/ae4696b0-d870-11f1-8249-bf1914cabd52/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-88cd0a37.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/ae4696b0-d870-11f1-8249-bf1914cabd52/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-88cd0a37.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">150beeaa-d870-11f1-9bf3-4f43ee797e95</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:00:09 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>US midterms bring a wave of historic firsts as minorities win key races</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/us-midterms-bring-a-wave-of-historic-firsts-as-minorities-win-key-races</link><description>

<![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:00:00 +0000 en <![CDATA[ NASA's Artemis II moon launch tore a hole in Earth's upper atmosphere so huge it disrupted GPS signals ]]> The launch of NASA's Artemis II mission in April 2026 caused significant disturbances in Earth's ionosphere that could have triggered temporary, localized errors in GPS positioning, a new study has found.

The study, by a team of researchers from National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan, analyzed data from high-precision networks of fixed, ground-based GPS receivers, used by U.S. scientific institutions to measure the minuscule motions of Earth's tectonic plates in the lead-up to earthquakes. By measuring how long it takes GPS signals to travel from space to ground stations, the researchers were able to reconstruct how the passage of the Artemis II mission's Space Launch System (SLS) rocket changed the concentrations of free electrons in the ionosphere — the electrically charged layer of Earth's atmosphere at altitudes above 30 miles (50 kilometers).

The measurements found that the ionospheric disturbances resulting from the sheer power of the Artemis II launch were more significant than any caused by other rocket launches to date and up to ten times more intense than those observed following the test launches of SpaceX's Starship, which is twice as powerful as the SLS based on liftoff thrust.

Artemis II saw humans return to the lunar space for the first time in more than fifty years, a mission that NASA hopes will pave the way for lunar landings and eventually the establishment of a sustained human presence on the moon.

During the mission's launch, ground-based GPS stations detected changes in the ionospheric electron density equivalent to positioning errors of several meters. Such inaccuracies could easily throw self-driving cars off track, potentially causing traffic collisions, according to Charles Lin, an earth science professor at National Cheng Kung University and one of the co-authors of the paper.

"A positioning error of a couple of meters is enough to cause an autonomous car to change lanes," Lin told Space.com. "It could have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning."

GPS receivers determine their position on Earth's surface at any single moment by measuring their distance to four different GPS satellites. When concentrations of free electrons in the upper atmosphere change — for example during a solar storm or after a rocket passage — the signal reaches Earth either faster or more slowly, resulting in inaccurate measurements.

Satellites of the U.S. GPS constellation and other Global Navigation Satellite Systems orbit Earth at an altitude of around 12,550 miles (20,200 kilometers), far above the upper edge of the ionosphere, meaning the positioning, navigation and timing signal these satellites transmit must pass through this volatile atmospheric layer to reach Earth.

Severe solar storms can disrupt GPS signals for days by dumping energy into the atmosphere in the form of charged particles from the sun. The impact of rocket launches, triggered by the supersonic flight of the rocket body through the high-altitude air, is much more short-lived. As the rocket soars up, it creates a shock wave, which virtually punches a hole into the ionosphere.

In the aftermath of the Artemis II launch, the researchers observed two such holes — one left behind by the 212-foot-long (65 meters) SSL core stage, and the other caused by two subsequent thruster burns of the rocket's upper stage. In both cases, these holes stretched across the American continent from East to West like giant 3,100-mile (5,000-kilometer) contrails.

Despite the enormous power of the SLS core stage, the disturbance caused by the second-stage burns directly inside the ionosphere was far more prominent.

Those two burns, at altitudes around 115 miles (185 kilometers), took place more than an hour after lift-off and allowed the Orion capsule to break free from Earth's gravity and head for the moon.

"Rocket launches from the ground to space produce that kind of effect, but we have never seen this kind of orbital maneuver in an interplanetary mission," said Lin. "In the future, as we are going to see many more missions going to the moon and to Mars, these space weather effects will become much more significant."

The study was published as a pre-print online in the journal Geophysical Research Letters.

]]> <![CDATA[ Students gather to explore Hawaii's glorious night sky | Space photo of the day for Nov. 4, 2026 ]]>

Students gathered under the stars in Hawaii recently to explore the awesome nature of the night sky together.

What is it?

From Oct. 19 to Oct. 22, more than 1,400 students on the Big Island of Hawaii gathered for the Journey Through the Universe event to explore astronomy together.

The Journey Through the Universe program is currently in its 23rd year. It was originally developed by the National Center for Earth and Space Science Education (NCESSE) and later introduced in Hawaii by the international Gemini Observatory, a program within the U.S. National Science Foundation's NOIRLab (National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory) that works with the Department of Education Hilo-Waiākea.

The program aims to introduce students in the Hilo-Waiākea public school system to astronomy as well as the incredible science that happens across Hawaii. The students who participate range from preschoolers to seniors in high school, so the program introduces some students to astronomy and helps others explore possible careers in STEM fields.

This year, the program brought in 19 volunteer educators from scientific institutions like Maunakea Observatories and supported hands-on activities and lessons that went from the classroom to under the Milky Way.

Why is it incredible?

This image shows a growing love for astronomy in progress. From the red glow of a skywatching night (red light doesn't interfere with our ability to see at night like white light does) to the scattered telescopes and students standing under the stars, this scene paints a larger picture.

This is just one program, but in bringing together volunteers, educators, scientists and students, the program has created an incredible and enduring learning experience.

Whether or not students walk away wanting to pursue a career in STEM, this incredible immersion in astronomy can help to foster a lifelong appreciation for science and nature. It's always a great idea to gather under the stars and explore together.

]]> <![CDATA[ Drone warfare in space: Swarms of autonomous, laser-shooting cubesats could defend Western satellites in orbit ]]> In May 2026, four Russian military satellites came close to ICEYE-X36, a private synthetic aperture radar satellite widely believed to be providing battlefield intelligence for Ukraine, in an apparently aggressive and risky "grey zone" maneuver that spooked many in the space industry.

Close enough to jam or interfere with the satellite's signal, blind it with a laser, fire a metal dart at it or, simply, force it to maneuver and burn fuel, the satellites' seemingly intimidatory behavior has increased the West's desire to develop defensive technology for satellites. In October 2026, it was reported that one of those same four Russian satellites passed within 500 meters (1,650 feet) of the same ICEYE satellite.

Now, U.K. startup Shield Space is racing to apply the lessons of drone warfare in Ukraine to develop swarms of up to 100 very small, low-cost, attritable drone-like autonomous spacecraft called cubesats. Released by a car-sized carrier in Earth orbit, these microwave-sized spacecraft will act as interceptors to protect Western satellites, and their deployment will mark a next step in the evolution of orbital warfare. Shield Space says that these space drones will use "effectors" like lasers or microwaves, or "kinetic standoff" techniques, to defend Western satellites even if controllers lose contact with them.

"We're talking about deploying 100 cubesats on a protect-and-defend mission for less than £100 million [$134 million US], which is how [much] you would pay for one satellite previously," said Graeme Ritchie, co-founder and CEO of Shield Space.

Launched in 2023, NASA's civilian project Starling demonstrated that a swarm of four small satellites can cooperate and operate autonomously in space on a civilian science mission without relying heavily on real-time commands from ground control. But that seems like a far cry from the adversarial or defensive missions Shield Space and its competitors imagine. It is telling that the leading space powers appear not to have demonstrated swarm combat in space — although they tend to be reluctant to reveal their space warfare capabilities.

In the fourth quarter of 2027, Shield Space plans to take this next step in space warfare's evolution by demonstrating rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) with two very small spacecraft. This effort, named Project Broadsword, will launch on SpaceX's Transporter-21 rideshare mission. It will send up an 8U cubesat and a smaller 3U target craft, which Shield Space plans to maneuver from 100 kilometers (62 miles) apart to within 100 meters (330 feet) of each other and, through four stages of autonomy, from human-in-the-loop to "approximately" fully autonomous. (A cubesat unit, or U, is a cube that measures 10 cm, or about 4 inches, on a side.)

The gaps between a true satellite-defense capability and this demonstration appear to be great, in terms of the technological and practical challenges of squeezing propulsion and power systems, AI compute power, sensors, the lasers the swarm needs to communicate and weapon systems onto small, lightweight maneuvering satellites. But it is a gap that Shield Space believes it can bridge through the purchase of relatively cheap off-the-shelf technology rather than more expensive bespoke designs.

"Yes, it's a problem because of size, weight and power," Ritchie told Space.com. "We've had to totally innovate from scratch some elements of the mission… but we have only got roughly 100 cm by 100 cm [40 by 40 inches], so saving space or having systems that are already completely integrated is the main aim."

"We have commissioned EnduroSat to build us an autonomous 8U cubesat that has chemical propulsion and its own imagery-collecting capability, which we will put our software on," said Dan Molland, co-founder and CTO of Shield Space, "and which we will then use to conduct our RPO.

"The good thing about cubesats is they're very standardized and they're very off the shelf," he added. "There's always some level of adjusting you've got to do, but these cubesats are a lot more plug and play than more conventional platforms, which are usually all custom-built."

Yet to focus on the technical issues may be to miss the point. "It takes an extraordinary amount of data to train the models and algorithms to achieve a fully autonomous mission," said Ritchie, "and the problem [unlike in the Ukraine war] is that data is not readily available.

"We can train AI using synthetic data, but it's just not quite good enough for space. It's incredibly important to gather data from missions like this if we really want autonomous missions in the future."

There is also the complexity of the AI needed in a war-fighting system. "Starling is a really great example," Molland told Space.com. "With Starling, you're essentially just asking a guidance system to make sure you stay within a given range of this or that satellite… But if you are controlling a swarm to deliver [a] military mission, you have a much more complex set of questions."

It also comes with the challenge of ensuring that AI complies with any rules of engagement.

But Ritchie and Molland believe these technical challenges can be overcome, and they have an aggressive schedule of demonstrations planned that they think will prove it.

Bleddyn Bowen, associate professor of astropolitics at Durham University in the U.K. and author of the book "War in Space: Strategy, Spacepower, Geopolitics" (Edinburgh University Press, 2020), is more cautious about Shield Space's plans for the evolution of space warfare.

"They remind me of a late Cold War missile-defense scheme called Brilliant Pebbles," he told Space.com. "It was one of the more advanced research and development programs in the Strategic Defense Initiative."

]]> <![CDATA[ The Taurid meteor shower peaks tonight — and fireballs could steal the show ]]> Heads up stargazers! The Taurid meteor shower is upon us, bringing multiple peaks of activity that could see spectacular shooting stars and fireballs brighten November's sky. Here's where and when to look.

What is the Taurid meteor shower(s)?

Every autumn, Earth plows through streams of debris left behind by Comet Encke, a 3-mile-wide (4.8-kilometer) ice body that orbits the sun once every 3.3 years.

These debris streams produce two branches of the Taurid meteor shower: The Southern Taurids, active from Sept. 20 to Nov. 20 and the Northern Taurids, active from Oct. 20 to Dec. 10.

As Earth plows through the debris streams, tiny particles slam into our atmosphere at 65,000 miles per hour (104,607 kilometers per hour), producing dazzling streaks of light across the night sky.

Both branches of the Taurid meteor shower appear to travel away from a point of origin — or radiant — located in the constellation Taurus, which rises in the southeastern sky during November evenings.

The Taurids are known for spawning brilliant fireball meteors, which can flare brighter than Venus as pebble-sized pieces of debris enter and burn up in the atmosphere.

When to look for Taurid shooting stars

The Southern Taurid shower features two distinct yearly peaks, the first of which occurred on Oct. 14. The second takes place overnight on Nov. 4-5 and is associated with an increase in fireball activity, when up to five meteors per hour could be seen blazing across the sky.

The Northern Taurid stream, meanwhile, is expected to peak overnight on Nov. 11-12 with the same predicted hourly rate of up to five meteors per hour streaking across the dark, near moonless sky.

How to spot Taurid meteors

Head out to a dark sky location around midnight on the night of the peaks, when the shower's radiant in the constellation Taurus is positioned high in the southeastern sky, maximizing the number of meteors that can be seen.

Remember not to stare directly at the radiant. Meteors seen close to the constellation Taurus strike our planet almost head-on, and so will have the shortest trails. Instead, pick out a patch of sky a little distance away, where the shooting stars will be at their most eye-catching as they skim through Earth's atmosphere.

Never use a telescope or binoculars to hunt for meteors, you want to take in as much of the sky as possible, not limit your field of view! And be sure to wrap up warm and allow 20-30 minutes for your eyes to adapt to the dark — a vital and often overlooked step for anyone hoping to catch even the faintest of meteors.

Hubble also regularly teams up with other telescopes for science work, and its observations have led to the publication of at least 23,000 scientific papers, NASA figures suggest. And, despite its age, Hubble remains in high demand. "Astronomers request about seven times as much observing time as is available each year," the agency stated in September.

Hubble is also widely appreciated by the public. People have long enjoyed and celebrated its iconic images, such as the Eagle Nebula's "Pillars of Creation," a gorgeous shot that has been revisited several times over the decades. As such, this is not the first time in recent years that discussions have opened about keeping the famed observatory running for a while longer.

In 2022, for example, billionaire tech entrepreneur Jared Isaacman proposed using SpaceX hardware to mount a Hubble-servicing mission. (Isaacman also purchased and commanded two crewed SpaceX missions to Earth orbit, which flew in September 2021 and September 2024.) NASA declined, however, citing possible risks to the healthy observatory.

Hubble will naturally enter the atmosphere in 2033 or 2034 due to orbital drag, so any attempt to service it would have to be in 2032, the agency stated.

That long-shot rescue mission — which was developed quickly to race against accelerated solar activity, which ballooned Earth's atmosphere and increased drag — launched successfully this summer. But control issues prevented Katalyst's LINK spacecraft from meeting up with Swift. Swift is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere tomorrow (Nov. 4) after 22 years of operations — far past its two-year design lifetime.

]]> <![CDATA[ Ancient star collisions could explain mysterious Little Red Dots and 'impossible' black holes ]]> New research suggests that collisions between stars in the early universe were common, which could help explain the rapid growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The team behind this research performed simulations of the early universe and found stellar systems were densely packed, leading to stars frequently slamming into each other. While rapid collisions would have destroyed the stars involved, slower collisions would have led to repeated mergers, creating single over-massive stars, which could collapse and form larger-than-usual black holes at the end of their lives. These could be the seeds of the first supermassive black holes.

Dense stellar environments do still exist in the modern universe at the hearts of galaxies; however, these aren't conducive to the types of collisions that would birth ultra-massive stars. That is because there are already supermassive black holes at the hearts of modern galaxies, and their immense gravitational influence speeds up orbiting stars, meaning collisions that do occur are high-speed and destructive, thus failing to birth overmassive stars.

"Perhaps the strangest outcome of our simulations is that stars can merge repeatedly within the cluster until they form one gigantic star with a mass equal to that of an entire cluster," team member Claire Williams, of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), said in a statement. "When a star this huge reaches the end of its life, models suggest that it may have no option but to collapse into itself and form a massive black hole."

My, haven't you grown? How did supermassive black holes get so big so fast?

The existence of supermassive black holes before the universe was even 1 billion years old is something that has puzzled astronomers since the JWST started spotting them in 2022.

This is because black holes should need at least 1 billion years to complete the feeding and merger processes that result in a "supermassive" status of possessing millions or billions of times the mass of the sun.

One suggestion put forward by scientists to explain this is that supermassive black holes don't start out from scratch. Instead, they form from black hole seeds called intermediate-mass black holes.

Normally, when a massive star collapses, it births a stellar-mass black hole possessing a mass between 10 and 100 times the mass of the sun. This is considerably smaller than supermassive black holes that dominate the hearts of all modern galaxies with masses millions to billions of times the mass of our star.

Intermediate-mass black holes are thought to sit between these two families of cosmic titans with masses between 100 and 100,000 times that of the sun. The problem is, no single star should have enough mass to collapse and create an intermediate-mass black hole. But that is valid only for the conditions we see in the "modern" 13.8-billion-year-old universe in our immediate cosmic vicinity. Conditions were very different further out into the universe and further back in time.

Indeed, such seeds emerged from these new simulations in environments of dense star clustering, which could solve this mystery by allowing those growth processes to get a head start.

"Dense star clusters provide a natural birthplace for massive black-hole seeds in our model," Williams said. "The same environment that forms the black hole can also provide stars and gas that influence its subsequent growth."

However, this could be a two-for-one deal. The JWST has also been routinely discovering astronomical bodies called Little Red Dots in the early universe. Little Red Dots are curious because they seem to have completely disappeared by the time the cosmos reached 2 billion years old.

Little Red Dots the cosmic elephant in the room

]]> <![CDATA[ Voting in space: NASA astronauts cast ballots from International Space Station ]]> The three Americans currently living off Earth just made sure their electoral voices were heard.

Anil Menon told us today (Nov. 3) that he and fellow NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins voted in the U.S. midterm elections from the International Space Station (ISS).

"Yes, you can even vote from space! All three U.S. crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials," Menon wrote in an X post this morning.

That post included a 29-second video, in which Menon — wearing, like many of us today, an "I voted" sticker — shows us his "voting booth."

It's actually his room on the ISS, Menon explained. "Inside of it is my computer, where I was able to fill out an electronic form and send it to Harris County so I could vote today," he said.

Most NASA astronauts register to vote in Texas' Harris County; it's home to Johnson Space Center in Houston, the agency's human spaceflight hub.

Americans have been able to vote from space since 1997, when Texas passed a law allowing this to happen. The first person to take advantage of the legislation was NASA astronaut David Wolf, who cast his ballot from Russia's Mir space station that same year. (The ISS didn't welcome its first crew until November 2000.)

"Just like any other American away from home, astronauts may fill out a Federal Post Card Application to request an absentee ballot," NASA officials wrote in an astronaut-voting explainer.

The process is somewhat involved, however.

"After an astronaut fills out an electronic ballot aboard the orbiting laboratory, the document flows through NASA's Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System to a ground antenna at the agency's White Sands Test Facility in Las Cruces, New Mexico," they added. "From New Mexico, NASA transfers the ballot to the Mission Control Center at NASA Johnson and then on to the county clerk responsible for casting the ballot. To preserve the vote's integrity, the ballot is encrypted and accessible only by the astronaut and the clerk."

The trio currently share the orbiting lab with four other people — Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and cosmonauts Anna Kikina, Pyotr Dubrov and Sergey Teteryatnikov. Kutryk and Teteryatnikov are members of Crew-13, whereas Dubrov and Kikina shared the Soyuz with Menon.

]]> <![CDATA[ 'OGame' developers explain how the browser-based sci-fi game has lasted 24 years ahead of the huge Orion update ]]> If you were on the Internet in the early 2000s looking for free browser games to play, OGame was a blooming sci-fi strategy sensation that couldn't be ignored. With online servers providing the structure for a living and evolving universe where players fought, traded, and created empires from scratch, its limited visual presentation was no issue.

Times have changed, but GameForge hasn't gone anywhere. OGame has been ported to mobile devices, and content updates have kept it alive and fresh for much longer than a plethora of installable MMO games.

With the Orion update, which will hit the newly launched universes (servers) on November 6, OGame is introducing conflicts against non-player-character (NPC) enemies, wave-based battles, co-op missions, and completely new systems that can also be disrupted by other players.

The game's endurance and such a major reinvention are stunning achievements, so we asked GameForge's Martin Liedtke (Director, Products of Browser Games) and Enrico Mareth (Senior Project Manager for OGame PC and Mobile) about the many challenges of working on OGame alongside the community for so long, what Orion is bringing to the table, and what's next for this worldwide phenomenon.

Some quotes have been editorialized and lightly trimmed for better flow.

"OGame has an enduring core: You build an interstellar empire, and your decisions matter... Keeping it fresh means adding meaningful choices to that foundation," said Liedtke. "Orion adds missions against automated opponents (PvE) alongside missions open to other players (PvP)... It supports different appetites for risk."

The GameForge veteran noted, however, that it's the community that "supplies another kind of freshness" after the studio releases the new content. "We develop the systems; players create much of the history."

Part of this approach is keeping tabs on how very different kinds of players approach what's available. "Some commanders concentrate on their economy; others enjoy expeditions or carefully coordinated fleet operations... Orion follows that approach; more experienced players can dig into fleet composition, progression, and cooperation. The aim is to offer worthwhile choices."

Liedtke also noted that "OGame's PvP has become a sophisticated contest of information and coordination" over time. Some players like to scout targets and organize combined attacks when enemy fleets are vulnerable. Those battles resolve automatically, but it's the planning that "can be remarkably intricate," especially after so many years of updates.

The PvE in Orion doesn't sacrifice any of those intricacies or density. In fact, it's adding a "more structured layer" that gives players clear objectives. In most cases, they'll have to cooperate to obtain better rewards. "There is a strong case for introducing that kind of cooperative PvE earlier. It gives players another reason to build and use fleets together."

Over two decades later, how people choose to engage with OGame has changed, pushing GameForge to consider supporting new platforms. Today, mobile devices have become essential to free-to-play games' success over time.

Mareth told us their importance "has made touch controls, navigation, and clarity on smaller screens central development considerations," even if thousands of players still remain attached to PC as their main platform. "We're currently working on a design overhaul of the app, combining what we've learned with players' feedback."

Liedtke also said there is more overlap between PC and mobile players than you might imagine.

"The same player might check their empire on a phone and spend a longer session planning in the browser." Liedtke also noted that "Different playstyles also have different needs," adding that activities like mining and trading fit "comfortably" into short mobile sessions, but complex fleet operations benefit from sitting in front of one's PC.

While it's a game of interstellar conflict and sci-fi spaceships, OGame does take a lot of inspiration from real-life science, even if it stretches that science well past its limits. "When ships are destroyed in battle, the debris field can form a moon around a player's planet," explains Liedtke. "The chance (of that happening) is linked to the real lunar cycle: it is higher around a full moon than a new moon."

He noted it's a "playful connection" to astronomy, "rather than a simulation of how real moons form," but the developers thought it was cool to influence the game via things that happen in our own sky.

This possible in-game "event" also led to one of the best examples of player ingenuity in OGame: Moonshots. Liedtke explained that "players organize deliberate battles and exchange sacrificial fleets to help one another obtain those valuable moons. They have turned destruction into a cooperative project. For a designer, the lesson is to examine what players can achieve together, as well as what an individual action rewards."

As the team figured out how to develop "the more imaginative side of science fiction" in OGame's universe, they also decided to explicitly use deuterium for fusion research and as fuel. Star Trek fans will recognize this as the starship fuel of that universe, but it is a real substance: one of two stable isotopes of hydrogen. "Those scientific references give the universe familiar foundations," remarks Liedtke.

In OGame's shared galaxy, Orion is introducing "anomalies" as a central new feature, which Liedtke described as "mission sites you uncover with a new scanner" before it's required to send in ships. "Combat missions ask you to hold position against waves of automated fleets; peaceful missions put your cargo ships to work collecting rewards." The twist is these missions are open to co-op... but also to rival commanders that can attack the objectives marked as PvP. While you can theoretically ignore them, better rewards await for daring commanders.

With PvE bringing all sorts of new design opportunities to the table, Liedtke pointed out the Orion update "gives us a foundation to learn which kinds of missions players find rewarding" as GameForge looks to the strategy MMO's future. "Personally, I would like to explore encounters that make commanders reconsider what to send and how to work together. Discovery becomes more interesting when it changes your plan."

Sounds exciting, though Liedtke quickly added that this isn't an official announcement of future features.

OGame's 25th anniversary is in 2027, and while the team is tight-lipped on what the team has planned, Liedtke noted that "Reaching a quarter of a century in 2027 will be an extraordinary moment for OGame. We owe that longevity to the team's continued work and, above all, to the players who keep building empires, forming alliances, and giving this universe its stories."

OGame is available on PC (via browser and GameForge's own platform) and on mobile devices via the App Store and Google Play. The Orion update arrives on November 6, 2026.

]]> <![CDATA[ Dimorphos in sight: Europe's Hera probe gets its 1st look at battered space rock (photo) ]]> Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart.

Hera is nearing the end of its voyage to the Didymos asteroid system, having launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in October 2024. The spacecraft snapped the image of Didymos and the smaller Dimorphos on Oct. 18 from a distance of 795 miles (1280 kilometers) from the pair, which are currently about 122 million miles (197 million km) from Earth.

"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," Michael Kueppers, Hera project scientist at the European Space Agency (ESA), said in a statement. "Before this acquisition, the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) smashed into Dimorphos in September 2022, changing the asteroid's orbit in a pioneering planetary defense demonstration. Hera's job is to survey the damage and refine our understanding of the impact, as well as the asteroids themselves.

Hera performed braking maneuvers earlier in October to slow its approach and put it on course to rendezvous with the binary system. The spacecraft is designed to make follow-up observations of the asteroids using 12 payloads, providing new insights that will prove valuable for planetary defense efforts. The mission also carries a pair of cubesats for a closer look and eventual landing on the 495-foot-wide (151 meters) Dimorphos.

For now, Hera is continuing its approach and preparing for arrival, with a big reveal expected to occur later this month.

"Our views will grow much sharper as Hera comes closer," said ESA's mission manager Ian Carnelli. "We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos — the first object in the solar system to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action — on 25 November."

<description>Dřív běžný plo&#353;ný růst mezd v IT už se nekoná, uvádí průzkum společností Grafton Recruitment a Gi Group.  <description>Na volebním lístku jsem nebyl, kdyby ano, drtivě bychom vyhráli, napsal Donald Trump o volební noci na své sociální síti.  <description>Demokraté slaví v amerických volbách do Kongresu historické úspěchy a v obou komorách parlamentu získají většinu. „Věřím v to, že se mezi demokraty a republikány utvoří cesta pro spolupráci,“ říká pro Radiožurnál Marek Koten, místopředseda české pobočky organizace Republicans overseas. „Jednou z prvních věcí bude najít cestu, jak zmírnit válku s Íránem,“ myslí si americký mediální konzultant a volič demokratů Brady Clough.</description>

 <description>USA zažívají politické zemětřesení. První všeobecné volby po návratu Donalda Trumpa do Bílého domu skončily převahou demokratů. Od ledna ovládnou Sněmovnu reprezentantů i Senát. V některých státech už se výsledky potvrdily. Republikáni ztratili tradiční státy jako Kansas, Texas nebo Jižní Karolínu. „Trumpova smířlivá povolební rétorika dlouho nevydrží,“ říká pro Český rozhlas Plus Tomáš Klvaňa z New York University in Prague.</description>

 <description>Počet obětí pondělního ruského útoku na centrum humanitární pomoci v obci Komyšuvacha v Záporožské oblasti vzrostl na 40, oznámil ve středu na telegramu ukrajinský prezident Volodymyr Zelenskyj. „Pod troskami může být ještě více než 30 lidí,“ dodal. Podle agentury Reuters jde o jeden z nejsmrtelnějších útoků na civilisty v tomto roce.</description>

 <description>Demokraté jasně vyhráli úterní volby do Kongresu. Ovládnou jak Sněmovnu reprezentantů, tak Senát. Poprvé po několika generacích navíc dosáhli vítězství i v tradičních baštách republikánů. Demokrat získal senátorské křeslo v Kansasu po 94 letech.  <description><ul class='text-md--m text-lg'><li>Poselství amerických voleb ze středečního rána jsou jednoznačná. Američané jsou nespokojení s tím, kudy se jejich země v posledních dvou letech ubírala, a dali to najevo jasněji, než průzkumy předvídaly.</li> <li></li> <li>Čistě na počet hlasů demokratičtí kandidáti porazili ty republikánské o 13 procentních bodů. Ani demokraté však nemají jednoduchý úkol – nezklamat voliče, kteří mají nemalá očekávání, že brzy pocítí změny.</li> </ul></description>

 <description>Kybernetický útok zasáhl několik krevních bank ve Francii, ale byl zmařen dříve, než mohl způsobit poškození krevních produktů nebo vzorků. Píše o tom ve středu agentura AP s odvoláním na úřady. Cílem útoku bylo zvýšit teploty na extrémně vysoké úrovně.</description>

 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/evropa-muze-byt-po-volbach-tercem-trumpovy-frustrace-mini-experti-ukrajina-se_2611041146_jho</link>
 <description>Spojenými státy se přehnala modrá vlna, demokraté ve volbách do Kongresu ovládli i tradiční republikánské bašty jako Texas či Kansas. Úředníci však falzifikát okamžitě odhalili. Místo nové práce tak muže kvůli podvodu čeká trestní stíhání.</description></item><item><title>Zbytečně riskují životy. Policisté na Jablonecku si posvítili na nebezpečné přejezdy</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/904886-zbytecne-riskuji-zivoty-policiste-na-jablonecku-si-posvitili-na-nebezpecne-prejezdy.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/904886-zbytecne-riskuji-zivoty-policiste-na-jablonecku-si-posvitili-na-nebezpecne-prejezdy.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:00:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Doprava</category><description>Jablonečtí dopravní policisté vyrazili do terénu, aby si posvítili na řidiče, kteří na rizikových železničních přejezdech bez závor ignorují značku STOP. V Desné přistihli dva hříšníky – řidič vyvázl s pokutou, řidička dokonce řídila přes zákaz.</description></item><item><title>Šestkrát na stupních vítězů. Piva ze Svijan uspěla na Žatecké dočesné</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904866-sestkrat-na-stupnich-vitezu-piva-ze-svijan-uspela-na-zatecke-docesne.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904866-sestkrat-na-stupnich-vitezu-piva-ze-svijan-uspela-na-zatecke-docesne.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:54:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Luboš Vrabec</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Hned šest medailových úspěchů si připsala svijanská piva na 69. ročníku tradiční Žatecké dočesné. Zcela například opanovala kategorii Silné pivo světlé, v níž obsadila první tři místa.</description></item><item><title>Oprava dopravního hřiště je u konce. Nově nabízí i kruhový objezd</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/904848-oprava-dopravniho-hriste-je-u-konce-nove-nabizi-i-kruhovy-objezd.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/904848-oprava-dopravniho-hriste-je-u-konce-nove-nabizi-i-kruhovy-objezd.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 14:45:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Luboš Vrabec</dc:creator><category>Doprava</category><description>V Liberci skončila kompletní rekonstrukce dopravního hřiště v Lužické ulici. Nové je dopravní značení i asfaltový povrch a přibyla také kruhová křižovatka.</description></item><item><title>Soud změnil výsledek voleb v Pulečném na Jablonecku, část hlasů nebyla započtena</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/904878-soud-zmenil-vysledek-voleb-v-pulecnem-na-jablonecku-cast-hlasu-nebyla.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/904878-soud-zmenil-vysledek-voleb-v-pulecnem-na-jablonecku-cast-hlasu-nebyla.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:45:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Politika</category><description>Pobočka krajského soudu v Liberci změnila výsledek komunálních voleb v Pulečném na Jablonecku. Při přepočtu hlasů soud zjistil, že čtvrtina z nich nebyla do výsledku započtená. Při porovnání původních a přepočtených výsledků byly zjištěny podstatné rozdíly v počtech hlasů.</description></item><item><title>Jizerská 50 trhá rekordy, hlavní závod se vyprodal nejrychleji v historii</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/sport/904772-jizerska-50-trha-rekordy-hlavni-zavod-se-vyprodal-nejrychleji-v-historii.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/sport/904772-jizerska-50-trha-rekordy-hlavni-zavod-se-vyprodal-nejrychleji-v-historii.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 10:45:00 +0100</pubDate><category>Sport</category><description>Jubilejní 60. ročník Jizerské 50 hlásí rekordní zájem. Kapacita hlavního závodu se naplnila za něco málo přes dva měsíce, rychle se plní také kratší tratě.</description></item><item><title>Liberečtí kriminalisté pátrají po uprchlém vězni. Nesnažte se ho zadržet, varují</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904835-liberecti-kriminaliste-patraji-po-uprchlem-vezni-nesnazte-se-ho-zadrzet-varuji.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904835-liberecti-kriminaliste-patraji-po-uprchlem-vezni-nesnazte-se-ho-zadrzet-varuji.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 08:54:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Krimi</category><description>Liberečtí policisté vyhlásili celostátní pátrání po 39letém vězni, který v neděli 1. listopadu utekl z pracoviště v ulici České Mládeže v Liberci. Může se pohybovat kdekoliv v regionu. Pokud muže spatříte, v žádném případě se ho nesnažte sami zadržet a ihned volejte tísňovou linku 158.</description></item><item><title>Geopark Český ráj přijde o značku UNESCO, nevyřešil problém s prodejem kamenů</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904834-geopark-cesky-raj-prijde-o-znacku-unesco-nevyresil-problem-s-prodejem.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904834-geopark-cesky-raj-prijde-o-znacku-unesco-nevyresil-problem-s-prodejem.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 06:30:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Geopark Český ráj se sídlem v Turnově přijde na konci letošního roku o prestižní značku UNESCO, kterou má od roku 2015. O jeho vyloučení v úterý rozhodla na svém zasedání Rada globálních geoparků UNESCO. Geopark ji nepřesvědčil, že vyřešil problém s prodejem drahých kamenů nejasného původu.</description></item><item><title>KOMENTÁŘ: Investiční návyky Čechů nemění jen inflace. Velký vliv mají i generační rozdíly</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/blogy-a-komentare/904643-komentar-investicni-navyky-cechu-nemeni-jen-inflace-velky-vliv-maji-i-generacni-rozdily.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/blogy-a-komentare/904643-komentar-investicni-navyky-cechu-nemeni-jen-inflace-velky-vliv-maji-i-generacni-rozdily.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 20:35:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Jan Dragon</dc:creator><category>Blogy a komentáře</category><description>Ekonomické otřesy posledních let, divoká inflace a skokový růst úrokových sazeb, nám všem daly tvrdou lekci. Ukázaly, že nechat úspory ležet na běžném účtu znamená sledovat, jak ztrácejí hodnotu. Čechy to donutilo přemýšlet jinak a celkový fondový kapitál u nás už přesáhl 2,33 bilionu korun.</description></item></channel></rss>

]]> Mandava Jazz / Mandau Jazz 2026 – Iva Bittová & Duo Jedlinský–Fischer https://www.vybezek.eu/296291-mandava-jazz-mandau-jazz-2026-iva-bittova-duo-jedlinsky-fischer/ Thu, 29 Oct 2026 18:16:24 +0000 https://www.vybezek.eu/?p=296291 Další večer u Kocoura – Mezinárodní hudební festival Mandava Jazz 2026 tentokrát ve středu 28. října 2026, opět ve varnsdorfském pivovaru Kocour, dorazila Iva Bittová a duo Jedlinský & Fischer.

Stejně jako nedávného Dana Bártu i Ivu Bittovou jsme už zažili několikrát (2011 na Vlčí hoře nebo 2017 v divadle). Vždy jako personu velmi osobitou, která si s nástrojem, hlasem a jazykem (nebo spíš jazyky, chvílemi to vypadalo na hudební esperanto-svahilštinu), dělá co chce. A vždy bravurně. Ačkoli ona sama je většinou tahákem na plakátech a v upoutávkách, sama sebe neupřednostňuje a dává spoustu prostoru všem, se kterými v tu kterou chvíli spolupracuje.

Iva Bittová – zpěv, housle; Jakub Jedlinský – akordeon, zpěv; Pavel Fischer – housle, zpěv

Inu, někdo je Fotograf a umí (snad) zachytit neuchopitelnou atmosféru, vyjádřit obrazem zážitek z hudby. Já mezi takové nepatřím, nejsem fotograf. Jsem jen přítomen.
